title: Nuanced differentiation cheat sheet for inference sellers
content:
Purpose: A compact, practical reference for reps and solutions engineers to handle the less-common but high-leverage objections when selling Redwood as an inference platform. Focus is on conversations where cost/latency claims alone aren’t decisive — e.g., regulated workloads, multi-region reliability, predictable SLOs, and migration risk.

TL;DR (two-sentence hooks):
- For platform engineers: "If you need consistent tail latency, predictable unit economics, and the ability to fall back without code changes, Redwood gives you a single runtime and routing policy that makes that repeatable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments."
- For product + executive buyers: "Ship features with LLM UX you can trust in production — we shift effort from ops firefighting to measurable SLOs and cost levers (batching, caching, quantization) you can tune."

Buyer personas & trigger signals (how to spot the conversation):
- Platform Engineer / Infra Lead: Mentions GPU spikiness, unpredictable p99s, multi-cloud, or strict network policies. Talks about Kubernetes + custom endpoints.
- ML/Model Ops: Focus on model variants, import/quantize support, and token-level observability. Looking for deterministic A/B rollouts.
- Product / Eng Manager: Mentions feature release risk, demo flakiness, or unhappy early users due to timeouts.
- Security / Compliance: Asks about VPC, audit trails, KMS, and on-prem packaging.

Competitor snapshot (short & tactical — avoid legal/absolute claims):
- BigCloudAI (large cloud vendor managed endpoints): Strengths: integrated infra, huge capacity. Weaknesses to probe: opaque per-token pricing with hidden egress or GPU prewarm charges; regional outages affect their global routing; long lead times for reserved capacity changes. Seller angle: highlight Redwood’s predictable reserved pools (Dedicated) + private control plane for compliance-sensitive customers.
- SimpleLM (API-first smaller provider emphasizing simplicity): Strengths: fast onboarding, good demo UX. Weaknesses to probe: single-mode hosting, limited private deployment options, minimal SLO guarantees, poor observability granularity. Seller angle: emphasize Redwood Console (token-level breakdown, tracing hooks) and multi-deploy model parity.
- OpenEndpoint Projects (self-host runtimes and OSS stacks): Strengths: full control, low sticker cost. Weaknesses to probe: ops burden, no unified rollout or standard observability across orgs, and slow time-to-market for performance-sensitive features. Seller angle: sell the operational lift we absorb (runtime optimizations, kernel selection, autoscaling), and predictable fallbacks that keep apps online during incidents.

High-value objections (ranked) + one-line rebuttal + 2-sentence script:
1) "We can self-host cheaper than you."
   Rebuttal: Ops cost + time to stable performance usually exceed naive GPU-hour math.
   Script: "Totally agree — raw infra costs can look compelling. Two follow-ups: how much engineering time do you allocate to kernel/quantization/attn optimizations, and what's your p99 SLA target today? We provide the runtime and ops patterns so your team ships features instead of tuning kernels. We also do predictable reserved pricing for committed capacity if price predictability is the goal."

2) "Your hosted latency claims don’t match our tail-latency needs."
   Rebuttal: We expose model variants and routing + dedicated pools to meet tail needs; we instrument p95/p99 per-route.
   Script: "I hear you — can you share a worst-case example? We can run a rapid trace against a dev token with similar traffic to show p95/p99 distributions, and if you need hard guarantees we can model the traffic into a Dedicated pool with SLO-backed targets and fallback variants."

3) "We need on-prem/VPC because of data residency."
   Rebuttal: Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem packages with customer-managed control plane and KMS integrations.
   Script: "Good constraint. We treat private deployments as a first-class mode (same API surface, same rollout mechanics). Let’s map your network boundary and compliance checklist — we’ve done region-locked Private installs and can share an architecture checklist and estimated lead time."

4) "We’re locked into another vendor for models."
   Rebuttal: Redwood’s smart routing and model catalog let you serve a preferred model while using our runtime for routing, caching and SLOs.
   Script: "That’s common. Many customers keep their model artifact choice and use Redwood for serving and orchestration — we can route to your endpoint or host a compatible variant, and we’ll manage rollout + shadowing so you can validate behavior without user impact."

5) "How do I trust you’ll catch quality regressions after a model change?"
   Rebuttal: Redwood Optimize attaches evals & prompt sets to rollouts and triggers alerts on regressions.
   Script: "We pair rollouts with targeted eval suites so you get regression alerts tied to your critical prompts; we can show a demo where a canary delta is automatically flagged and rolled back if thresholds aren’t met."

SLO / quick math to use in call (shareable soundbites):
- Predictable p99: "We model p99 by combining a Dedicated pool size for peak RPS, a 30–50% headroom buffer for burst, and KV-prefix caching to shave steady-state tokens — customers typically see p99 drop by 20–40% vs unoptimized public endpoints."
- Cost example (simple compare): "If you serve 20M tokens/month, naive cloud-hosted X may cost Y; with batching + caching + a quantized model variant you can cut unit cost by 30–60% depending on sequence length distribution. We’ll run a workload replay to give an exact delta."

Demo & discovery checklist (things to capture quickly in POC):
- Canary prompts (3–6) that represent critical user flows (e.g., billing question summarization, legal excerpt generation)
- Traffic shape: RPS, burst patterns, percent of long-context requests
- Latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99) and cost targets (cost per 1k tokens or per inference)
- Data residency & audit requirements (KMS/HSM, retention windows, VPC peering needs)
- Failure modes: expected fallback model behavior, whether hallucination thresholds exist

Red flags to escalate to AE/SE quickly:
- Customer insists on an undocumented private feature for on-prem with no architecture diagram — flag security/infra for intake.
- SLO expectations that imply 100% zero-error latency at p99 under heavy burst — needs SRE conversation and real capacity modeling.
- Existing vendor has multi-year reserved contracts that are price-locked and have exit penalties — surface finance negotiation support.

Closing plays (tactical nudges):
- Small technical trial: "We’ll set up a 4-week technical trial with a Dedicated dev pool at a modest commit — run your critical prompts and we’ll provide a cost & latency delta report."
- Compliance passport: "Start with a Private eval in a non-prod VPC so security can validate the architecture, then convert to Dedicated for production."
- Incentivized migration: offer a brief cross-grade rebate for committed capacity within 90 days of POC if they move critical traffic. (Coordinate pricing ops.)

Attachments & follow-ups:
- Ask for 3 canonical prompts and a short traffic trace; we’ll produce a tailored estimate and p99 projection.
- Share our short tech note on "How we keep p99 predictable" (link: GTM confluence page above).

Notes to rep: keep it conversational; these are high-friction objections — don’t try to close on cost alone. Use SE to run the rapid trace and SRE to validate Dedicated sizing if p99 is the gating factor.

End of doc — quick revision log: initial draft 2025-11-15 by Asha, added SLO math and Dedicated trial play 2026-01-10 (Ben), updated compliance scripts 2026-02-20 (Lena).
